title: Pauri 31: storehouses everywhere
hookLine: aasan loe loe: His seat and storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all (Japji 31)

cards: You've seen the photos: grocery shelves stripped bare because everyone got scared at the same time. Toilet paper gone, bread gone, one sad can of beans. Fear of running out makes people grab.
Now cut open one apple and count the seeds. Five, maybe eight. Each could grow a tree, and each tree could drop hundreds of apples a year for decades.
One apple holds an orchard. The world is stocked in a way that's hard to take in, and most days it goes unnoticed behind the worry about the shelves. Pauri 31 is about the storehouses.

teach.b: Pauri 31 is short, and it opens with a yogi's word. Aasan loe loe bhanddaar. Aasan is a seat, the mat or skin a yogi carried and sat on to meditate.
Wherever he went, his aasan went too, and that spot became his place. Guru Nanak says the One's aasan is loe loe, in world after world. There's no single spot to travel to.
Bhanddaar: storehouses. In Pauri 29, compassion was the bhanddaaran, the keeper of the stores. In Pauri 30, one of the three powers was the bhanddaaree, the one who sustains.
Now the storehouses themselves are in every world. Then today's line: jo kichh paaiaa su ekaa vaar. Whatever was put in, was put in once.

teach.h: FILLED ONCE, NOT IN A PANIC.
teach.b: Commentators read it as a creation already provided for: the stores filled at the start, not in a panic every morning.

teach.h: THE MAKER WATCHES WHAT WAS MADE.
teach.b: Kar kar vekhai sirjanhaar: having made it, the Creator watches over it, the same care as yesterday. Sache kee saachee kaar: true is the work of the True One.
And the refrain, one last time: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. With that, Nanak's answer to the yogis is complete.
Their earrings, their meal, their horn, their seat: each one turned toward the One who is everywhere. Tomorrow, the Japji starts to climb.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 31 closes the four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and its picture of storehouses in every world is often recalled as a teaching on trust and contentment.

o: a storehouse of grain and goods
a bright cloth tied on a flagpole

games.q: what's inside Pauri 31 — tap the pairs.
p: the yogi's seat, now in every world

s: Pauri 31 says the storehouses must be refilled every day
jo kichh paaiaa su ekaa vaar: whatever was put in, was put in once.
aasan is the word for a yogi's meditation seat
Nanak says the One's seat is in world after world.
Pauri 31 is the last of the four stanzas answering the yogis
pauris 28 to 31 each end with aades tisai aades.

games.q: a yogi carries his seat, his aasan, from place to place. where does Pauri 31 say the One's seat is?
games.why: aasan loe loe: in every world. there's no single spot to travel to; the seat is everywhere.

practice: Look at one place you can see or picture, a window with a tree in it, a kitchen shelf, your own hands, as a storehouse: leaves, light, grain, breath, years of work in your fingers.
Don't count what's missing; notice what's already there, and let it be more than you expected. Then breathe, one easy breath after another, drawing from a store you didn't fill.

wordCard.voice: Aasan, the yogi's seat. His seat and His storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all, and the Maker watches over what was made. The last answer to the yogis.
